label: Pesher Habakkuk (Commentary on Habakkuk) — Complete
summary_plain: Pesher Habakkuk is a continuous commentary on the prophetic book of Habakkuk, interpreting its words as prophecy about the community’s own time. The Kittim are the instrument of YHWH’s judgment — they come from afar, swift and violent, conquering all lands. The Teacher of Righteousness received from YHWH’s mouth the interpretation of the prophets’ words. The Wicked Priest pursued the Teacher of Righteousness to swallow him up on the Day of Atonement. The righteous shall live by his faithfulness — this applies to those who observe the Torah in the house of Yehudah, whom YHWH will deliver because of their toil and their faithfulness to the Teacher of Righteousness.
summary_scholarly: 1QpHab (Pesher Habakkuk) was among the first seven scrolls discovered in Cave 1 in 1947. It is the best-preserved pesher and the most important text for understanding the Qumran hermeneutical method. The commentary covers Habakkuk 1-2 verse by verse. The Kittim are identified as Rome — they sacrifice to their standards, they come from the coastlands, they conquer by systematic military force. The Teacher of Righteousness is YHWH’s chosen interpreter of the prophets. The Wicked Priest is a Jerusalem priest who initially walked in truth but was corrupted by wealth and power. Habakkuk 2:4 (‘the righteous shall live by his faithfulness’) is interpreted as applying specifically to Torah-observers faithful to the Teacher. The pesher method assumes that the prophets wrote about the future — the community’s own time — and that YHWH revealed the meaning to the Teacher of Righteousness.

key_terms.definition: Commentary on Habakkuk — 1QpHab, one of the original seven Cave 1 scrolls. A continuous pesher on Habakkuk chs 1-2, interpreting the oracle against Chaldea as a prophecy about the community's situation: Kittim (Rome), the Wicked Priest, and the revelation given to the Teacher of Righteousness.

The major antagonist of Pesher Habakkuk — a Jerusalem high priest who was legitimate at first but became corrupt. He pursued the Teacher of Righteousness, appeared at the Teacher's place of exile on Yom Kippur to confuse the community's fast, and was eventually punished by YHWH through the Kittim.

In Pesher Habakkuk, Kittim refers to Rome — the instrument of YHWH's judgment against the Wicked Priest and the corrupt establishment. The Kittim are powerful, swift, terrifying, and they will execute judgment — but they serve YHWH's purposes even in their brutality.

In Pesher Habakkuk, the Teacher of Righteousness is the one to whom YHWH revealed 'all the mysteries of the words of his servants the prophets.' The Teacher's specific role: unlocking the hidden meaning of prophecy through divine revelation. This is the Teacher's unique pesher authority.

Pesher Habakkuk col.7:1-5 states that YHWH revealed to the Teacher of Righteousness all the mysteries of the prophets' words. This divine revelation is the basis of the pesher method — the Teacher did not reason his way to the interpretation; YHWH directly disclosed it to him.

An event described in Pesher Habakkuk: the Wicked Priest appeared at the Teacher's place of exile on the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) to disrupt the community's fast and mislead them. This attack on the community's most sacred day illustrates the depth of the Wicked Priest's corruption.

The Cave 1 designation for Pesher Habakkuk — one of the original seven 1947 scrolls. Unlike most pesharim (found in Cave 4), Pesher Habakkuk comes from Cave 1 and is exceptionally well preserved — the best-preserved continuous pesher in the DSS corpus.

Pesher Habakkuk's interpretation of Habakkuk 2:4 ('the righteous shall live by his faithfulness/emunah'): the community understands this as those who observe the Torah and trust in the Teacher of Righteousness's interpretation. This is the community's covenant life — faithful observance anchored in the Teacher's revealed interpretation.

Pesher Habakkuk col.7:9-14 discusses the delay of the final appointed time: even if it delays, wait for it, it will surely come. The community addressed the theological problem of a delayed eschatological fulfillment by trusting in YHWH's timing.

A central Pesher Habakkuk theology: YHWH uses the terrifying Kittim (Rome) as his instrument of judgment against the corrupt Wicked Priest and the Jerusalem establishment. The enemy is simultaneously horrifying and divinely purposeful.

faq.question: What is Pesher Habakkuk?
faq.answer: Pesher Habakkuk (1QpHab) is a continuous commentary on the first two chapters of Habakkuk, found as one of the original seven Cave 1 scrolls from 1947. It is the best-preserved pesher in the DSS corpus. The text applies Habakkuk's oracle against the Chaldeans to the community's own time: the Kittim (Rome), the Wicked Priest (a corrupt Jerusalem high priest), and the Teacher of Righteousness's divine revelation.

faq.question: Who is the Wicked Priest in Pesher Habakkuk?
faq.answer: The Wicked Priest is a Jerusalem high priest who, according to the pesher, was legitimate at first ('called by the name of truth at the beginning of his standing') but became corrupt through wealth, arrogance, and betrayal of the covenant. He actively persecuted the Teacher of Righteousness, appearing at the Teacher's place of exile on Yom Kippur to disrupt the community's fast. He was eventually punished by YHWH through the Kittim (Rome). Various historical high priests have been proposed as candidates — the question of his exact identity remains debated.

faq.question: What is the Teacher of Righteousness's role in Pesher Habakkuk?
faq.answer: In Pesher Habakkuk col.7, the Teacher is described as the one to whom YHWH revealed 'all the mysteries of the words of his servants the prophets.' This is the Teacher's unique authority: not human learning or priestly lineage alone, but direct divine revelation of prophetic meaning. The Teacher does not interpret Habakkuk by reasoning; YHWH disclosed the oracle's true meaning to him. This divine-revelation basis is what distinguishes the pesher method from ordinary commentary.

faq.question: How does Pesher Habakkuk interpret Habakkuk 2:4?
faq.answer: Habakkuk 2:4 says 'the righteous shall live by his emunah (faithfulness/faith).' The pesher interprets this as: those who observe the Torah and trust in the Teacher of Righteousness's interpretation. Life comes from faithful Torah observance anchored in the Teacher's revealed interpretation. The NT later uses this same verse (Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11) for a different theological framework. The pesher's interpretation is earlier: the verse is about covenant faithfulness in the community's specific situation, not an abstract principle of individual faith.

faq.question: What does the Yom Kippur attack reveal about the Wicked Priest?
faq.answer: The Wicked Priest appeared at the Teacher's place of exile on the Day of Atonement specifically to disrupt the community's fast and mislead them. This is not a coincidental visit — Yom Kippur was the most sacred day of the year, the day of covenant renewal and atonement. By attacking on this day, the Wicked Priest demonstrated the depth of his corruption: he was willing to desecrate the holiest moment to strike at the Teacher. The pesher uses this event to confirm the Wicked Priest's judgment by YHWH.

faq.question: What is the theological significance of the Kittim in Pesher Habakkuk?
faq.answer: The Kittim (Rome) are both terrifying enemies and YHWH's instruments of judgment. This is a classic prophetic pattern: YHWH uses a foreign power to execute judgment on his own corrupt people. The Kittim do not know they serve YHWH's purposes; they act from their own imperial drive. But their power is ultimately accountable to YHWH's design. This framework allows the community to understand Roman power without despair: Rome is not outside YHWH's sovereignty — it is working within it, however unwittingly.

faq.question: How does the 'delay of the end' discussion in 1QpHab function?
faq.answer: The community expected an eschatological end that had not yet arrived by the time Pesher Habakkuk was composed. This delay was a real theological problem. The pesher addresses it by citing Habakkuk 2:3: 'even if it delays, wait for it; it will surely come.' The delay is reframed not as a failure of prophecy but as a test of faithful waiting. The community that waits faithfully is the righteous community; the ones who abandon waiting are those without genuine covenant faith.

faq.question: Why does Pesher Habakkuk stop at chapter 2?
faq.answer: Habakkuk chapter 3 is a psalm — a prayer of Habakkuk with musical notation. The DSS pesher method works on prophetic oracles, not psalms. The pesher commentary applied to chapters 1 and 2 (the oracle) but the psalm in chapter 3 was treated differently. Its absence from 1QpHab is consistent with the pesher method's focus on oracular/prophetic prose rather than liturgical poetry.

faq.question: How does Pesher Habakkuk compare to Pesher Nahum?
faq.answer: Both are continuous pesharim applying ancient prophets to the community's current situation. Pesher Nahum is unique in naming historical figures (Demetrius); Pesher Habakkuk consistently uses code names (Wicked Priest, Teacher of Righteousness, Kittim). Both interpret Kittim as Rome in their later layers. Pesher Habakkuk is from Cave 1 and far better preserved; Pesher Nahum is from Cave 4. Pesher Habakkuk has the most developed Teacher of Righteousness portrait in the DSS corpus.

faq.question: What does Pesher Habakkuk tell us about the community's approach to prophecy?
faq.answer: Prophecy in Pesher Habakkuk is never self-interpreting — it requires the Teacher's divinely given key. The prophets themselves did not fully understand what they wrote ('the Teacher of Righteousness was told all the mysteries of the prophets' words'). Ancient prophecy was encrypted foreknowledge; the Teacher's revelation unlocked the encryption for the community's time. This is a distinctive prophetic epistemology: scripture's meaning is hidden until YHWH reveals it to the right interpreter.
